title: The Side the Scalp Could See — Simultaneous Scalp vs. Stereo-EEG Seizure Detection (Gunnell 2025), 51-Second Contralateral Scalp Lag & ICU Peripheral Nerve Stimulator EEG Artifacts

teenKit.tldr: When doctors record brain activity simultaneously from deep inside the brain and from the scalp surface, they can see a 51-second delay and even a fake opposite-side reading during a seizure. This happens because the skull and thick tissues act like heavy sound-proofing walls, blurring and trapping deep electrical signals before they ever reach the surface.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding this bizarre physics gap stops doctors from making tragic surgical mistakes by realizing that surface-level scans can completely misrepresent what is actually happening deep inside the human mind.
keyTakeaways: Stereo-EEG electrodes planted deep in the brain catch electrical seizures instantly, while surface scalp electrodes might take nearly a minute to register the activity.
A seizure starting on the left side of the deep brain can trick scalp monitors into screaming loudest on the right side due to how electricity bends and diffuses through layers of bone and tissue.
ICU medical gear, like peripheral nerve stimulators, can pump out electrical static that completely mimics a terrifying brain seizure on a monitor if you don't know what you're looking at.

vocab.meaning: A method of tracking electrical activity in the brain using sensors placed either on the scalp or surgically implanted deep inside.
A mind-bending medical paradox where a deep brain monitor and a surface scalp monitor point to completely opposite sides of the head for the exact same event.
The frustrating time delay it takes for a deep electrical wave to painfully bleed through bone and tissue to show up on the opposite side of the skull's surface.
The way the skull, spinal fluid, and scalp naturally act like heavy insulation, dampening and scattering electrical signals before they hit surface sensors.

quiz.question: If a seizure starts on the left side of the deep brain, why might a standard scalp EEG show the strongest signal on the right side?
options: The computer system running the hospital monitors is usually hacked or glitched.
Electrical signals bend and diffuse unpredictably as they struggle through thick layers of skull and tissue.
The patient's brain actually flipped sides midway through the medical procedure.
Surface electrodes only pick up sound waves instead of electrical voltages.
quiz.explanation: The skull and tissue act as a messy filter, causing electrical currents to spread out and trick surface sensors into misjudging the origin point.

quiz.question: What does a 51-second delay between an intracranial monitor and a scalp monitor reveal about medical technology?
options: Surface scalp EEG is completely useless and should be thrown out of hospitals immediately.
Both monitors tell the truth, but they are answering totally different physical questions about the brain.
Deep brain wires always experience massive electrical slowdowns due to battery issues.
Seizures always take exactly 51 seconds to travel from the left hemisphere to the right.
quiz.explanation: Both screens are objectively accurate, but one tracks the source in the basement while the other tracks the echo on the roof.

quiz.question: What is an ICU peripheral nerve stimulator artifact capable of doing to an EEG reading?
options: It can completely cure a patient's epilepsy within minutes.
It can permanently melt the electrodes attached to a patient's scalp.
It can generate electrical noise that looks identical to a violent brain seizure on a monitor.
It can safely teleport electrical currents directly into the brain's deepest folds.
quiz.explanation: External medical gear can pump out sharp electrical pulses that mimic brain seizures, fooling clinicians into false alarms.
